One group of customers matters to Booking Holdings (BKNG) stock more than it may seem: the top members of its Genius loyalty program. Booking.com may look like a site travelers find through Google, but management says these members return more consistently and book directly more often than travelers outside Genius. Even so, the stock lost 29.0% in the year to October 28, 2026, as the S&P 500 returned 14.0%. So how many of Booking's room nights do these members book?

Top Genius Members Book Most Of Booking's Room Nights

Level 2 and Level 3 Genius members made up more than 30% of Booking's active customers in the June quarter. They accounted for what management called "a high 50% share" of its room nights, and management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that both figures were up from a year earlier.

These members also plan their trips further in advance than travelers outside Genius, and management said it sees room to strengthen the Genius offering further. So, as of the June quarter, Booking's most loyal customers were both a large part of its business and a growing one.

Is Booking Holdings Losing Travelers To AI Search?

Not on the whole, so far. Management said on the fiscal Q2 2026 call that direct room nights kept growing over the four quarters to June, with the direct share of consumer room nights staying in the mid-60% range.

Separately, could Tesla make their product more tangible? See: How Musk's Massive Marketing Miss Cost Tesla $10 Trillion.

The worry for any online travel company is that AI tools will answer travel questions themselves and send fewer travelers to booking sites. Booking does feel some of that: management said pressure on its traffic from unpaid search results continued in the June quarter, and that Google's AI overview had probably added to it. But management also said unpaid search remains a small part of Booking's room nights, and traffic from large language models, paid and unpaid, was still well below 1% of them.

Booking is also putting money into a tool of its own. On October 14, 2026, the company announced a planned $100 million investment in Vayo, its new company offering a personal travel agent that learns how you travel. So far, Booking's direct business is holding steady as the way people search for travel shifts. Investors are less sure: on September 23, 2026, Booking shares fell with other travel stocks on fears that Muse, Meta's AI agent, could let travelers bypass booking sites.

Wall Street expects a year-over-year increase in earnings on higher revenues when Airbnb, Inc. (ABNB) reports results for the quarter ended September 2026. While this widely-known consensus outlook is important in gauging the company's earnings picture, a powerful factor that could impact its near-term stock price is how the actual results compare to these estimates.

The earnings report, which is expected to be released on November 5, might help the stock move higher if these key numbers are better than expectations. On the other hand, if they miss, the stock may move lower.

While the sustainability of the immediate price change and future earnings expectations will mostly depend on management's discussion of business conditions on the earnings call, it's worth handicapping the probability of a positive EPS surprise.

Zacks Consensus Estimate

This company is expected to post quarterly earnings of $2.89 per share in its upcoming report, which represents a year-over-year change of +30.8%.

Revenues are expected to be $4.75 billion, up 16% from the year-ago quarter.

Estimate Revisions Trend

The consensus EPS estimate for the quarter has been revised 0.05% lower over the last 30 days to the current level. This is essentially a reflection of how the covering analysts have collectively reassessed their initial estimates over this period.

Investors should keep in mind that the direction of estimate revisions by each of the covering analysts may not always get reflected in the aggregate change.

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise

Price, Consensus and EPS Surprise Chart for ABNB
Earnings Whisper

Estimate revisions ahead of a company's earnings release offer clues to the business conditions for the period whose results are coming out. This insight is at the core of our proprietary surprise prediction model -- the Zacks Earnings ESP (Expected Surprise Prediction).

The Zacks Earnings ESP compares the Most Accurate Estimate to the Zacks Consensus Estimate for the quarter; the Most Accurate Estimate is a more recent version of the Zacks Consensus EPS estimate. The idea here is that analysts revising their estimates right before an earnings release have the latest information, which could potentially be more accurate than what they and others contributing to the consensus had predicted earlier.

Thus, a positive or negative Earnings ESP reading theoretically indicates the likely deviation of the actual earnings from the consensus estimate. However, the model's predictive power is significant for positive ESP readings only.

A positive Earnings ESP is a strong predictor of an earnings beat, particularly when combined with a Zacks Rank #1 (Strong Buy), 2 (Buy) or 3 (Hold). Our research shows that stocks with this combination produce a positive surprise nearly 70% of the time, and a solid Zacks Rank actually increases the predictive power of Earnings ESP.

title: How Big Could Airbnb Stock's Next Fall Be?
detail:
How Big Could Airbnb Stock's Next Fall Be?

Airbnb (ABNB) stock fell 4.6% in the week to October 27, 2026, while the S&P 500 edged up 0.14%. The shares now trade 11.4% below their highest close of the past year. For anyone holding the stock, the bigger worry is what a market-wide sell-off would do. When the whole market has fallen before, how far did Airbnb stock drop, and how long did it take to come back?

How Far Airbnb Stock Fell In Past Market Shocks

Since its shares began trading in December 2020, Airbnb has weathered five market shocks. The stock recorded its largest fall during the 2022 inflation shock, as the Fed tightened. In that period, the shares dropped 48%, while the S&P 500 lost 24%. Across all five shocks, Airbnb fell 28.0% on average, against a 13.4% decline for the index.

Recovery times varied widely. The shares needed a median of 6.3 months to climb from a low back to their earlier high. Two of those waits ran past a year. Airbnb took 16.0 months to recover from the 2025 US tariff shock. After the 2022 shock, the wait stretched to 49.7 months, and the stock only got back to that high in August 2026.

How Does Airbnb's Business Compare With A Year Ago?

Airbnb is growing faster than it was a year ago. Revenue rose 16.5% in the quarter ended June 30, 2026, outpacing the 12.7% growth posted in the same quarter of 2025. Over the past twelve months, sales reached $13.2 billion, up 13.6% from the twelve months before.

The company's operating margin improved in that quarter, but the measure remains lower over the full twelve months. The margin reached 21.0% in the June quarter, up from 19.8% a year earlier. Over the past twelve months it was 20.8%, against 22.5% in the preceding twelve-month window. Airbnb also holds far more cash than debt, reporting $12.1 billion in cash and short-term investments at the end of June 2026 against $2.5 billion of debt.

What Risks Is Airbnb Facing Now?

Airbnb faces the prospect of tighter rules in Europe, pressure on its prices, and a profit margin that management expects to slip slightly in the September quarter. News reports on September 9, 2026, indicated that new EU plans would give European cities more leeway to curb short-term rentals such as Airbnb. On an August 6, 2026, call, management called policy a risk, but not an existential one, that the company will manage forever.

At the time of that call, about half of Airbnb's active listings were on a single service fee. Management expects all of its listings to adopt the fee by the end of 2026, and said this fee puts downward pressure on pricing, an effect management wants so that Airbnb offers guests more value and stays priced competitively against other platforms. For the full year, management expects its implied take rate, the share of bookings Airbnb keeps as revenue, to be relatively flat against 2025. That outlook accounts for higher customer incentives tied to new businesses.

Choosing between a high-growth travel platform and a legacy retailer in transition requires balancing profitability against deep value. Is Airbnb Inc. (NASDAQ:ABNB) or GameStop Corp. (NYSE:GME) the better choice for your portfolio today?

Airbnb revolutionized the lodging market through its peer-to-peer network, while GameStop is navigating a shift from physical software to a digital-first entertainment model. Both companies have worked to streamline operations, yet they represent very different risk-reward profiles for everyday investors looking to allocate capital in the current market.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a global online marketplace that connects hosts with travelers looking for unique stays or local experiences. The company has established itself as a leader among travel and tourism stocks by offering an alternative to traditional hotels. By leveraging a network of over 5 million hosts to offer more than 9 million active listings, the business maintains a flexible platform that scales quickly. Note that Airbnb currently outsources a large majority of its community support operations to third-party providers.

In its latest annual report filed for FY 2025, revenue reached about $12.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 10.8% compared to the previous year. This expansion was supported by high net income of about $2.5 billion. The company reported a net margin of roughly 20.4%, which shows the percentage of revenue remaining as profit after all expenses are paid. While this was a slight decrease from the prior year, it remains a healthy figure for the travel services industry.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the debt-to-equity ratio was roughly 0.3x. This ratio measures total debt relative to what shareholders own, suggesting the company maintains a conservative level of borrowing. Its current ratio, which tracks the ability to pay short-term bills using short-term assets, was close to 1.4x. Free cash flow for the period reached around $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since stock-based compensation is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement.

The case for GameStop

GameStop serves as a specialty retailer for the gaming community, selling physical and digital games, collectibles, and hardware. The company operated approximately 2,206 leased stores as of late January 2026, while also pursuing additional sales through its e-commerce platforms. Its business model relies heavily on relationships with major manufacturers and publishers. In fiscal 2025, partners like Nintendo Co. (OTC:NTDOF), Sony Group Corp. (NYSE:SONY), and Pokémon accounted for a majority of the new products the company purchased.

detail:
Airbnb vs. Five Below: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?

Airbnb (NASDAQ:ABNB)and Five Below (NASDAQ:FIVE)both compete for discretionary consumer dollars, but they do so through entirely different business models. Choosing between them requires weighing the digital scale against the physical retail expansion.

Airbnb dominates the alternative accommodation space with millions of active listings, while Five Below focuses on low-price, trend-right goods for kids and teens. Investors often compare them because both represent growth-oriented plays within the consumer cyclical sector, albeit with different risk profiles and capital requirements.

The case for Airbnb

Airbnb operates a global marketplace for travel and tourism stocks, connecting more than 5.5 million hosts with guests seeking short-term stays. The company has moved beyond simple lodging to include Experiences and property management tools through its Co-Host Network. Its business model is capital-light, as it does not own the properties on its platform and relies on Apple for critical app distribution.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $12.3 billion, representing growth of approximately 10.8% over the previous fiscal year. Net income for the same period was roughly $2.5 billion, resulting in a net margin of close to 20.4%. This net margin, which measures how much profit a company keeps for every dollar of sales, reflects the high profitability inherent in a digital marketplace.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio was roughly 1.4x, which measures a company's ability to cover short-term debts with its current assets. The debt-to-equity ratio was close to 0.3x, indicating a conservative level of debt relative to shareholder equity. Free cash flow for FY 2025 was nearly $4.6 billion. Note that stock-based compensation accounted for roughly 34.3% of operating cash flow, inflating reported cash generation, since SBC is a non-cash expense added back to cash flow.

The case for Five Below

Five Below is a value retailer that organizes its stores into eight distinct "worlds," such as Style, Tech, and Candy. The company targets kids, pre-teens, and value-oriented shoppers, operating over 1,900 stores across 46 states. It is a prominent name among retail stocks because of its ability to quickly capitalize on viral trends while maintaining low price points for its core demographic.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $4.8 billion, representing nearly 22.9% growth over the prior year. Net income for the fiscal period was close to $358.6 million, and the company reported a net margin of roughly 7.5%. While lower than software-based businesses, this margin reflects the costs of sourcing physical inventory and managing a vast network of brick-and-mortar locations.

Investors choosing between established prestige and high-growth disruption face a compelling choice in 2026. Comparing American Express (NYSE:AXP) and Nu (NYSE:NU) reveals two distinct ways to capture global financial trends.

American Express relies on its premium brand to serve affluent spenders and large corporate clients worldwide. Meanwhile, Nu has emerged as a powerhouse in digital banking, rapidly acquiring millions of users across Latin America. This comparison examines whether the stability of a credit veteran or the momentum of a digital challenger is the better buy today.

The case for American Express

American Express operates as an integrated payments company, providing credit cards and travel services to individuals and businesses. Its strategy focuses on a premium customer base, which includes strategic partnerships with Delta Air Lines, Marriott International, and Airbnb. While the company serves large corporations, it also caters to small businesses, though it recently identified its portfolios for Amazon as held for sale.

In FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $72 billion, representing growth of approximately 10% compared to the previous year. The company generated a net income of roughly $10.8 billion during this period. This resulted in a net margin of about 16%, reflecting the company's ability to remain profitable while expanding its merchant network to over 170 million locations globally.

As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the company carries a debt-to-equity ratio of 1.7x. This ratio measures total debt relative to shareholder equity, indicating the level of leverage used to fund operations. Its current ratio is approximately 0.3x, which measures its ability to cover short-term liabilities with liquid assets. Free cash flow for the period was nearly $16.0 billion, providing significant capital for dividends and reinvestment.

The case for Nu

Nu operates as a digital financial services platform and is a leader among fintech stocks in Latin America. The company serves over 131 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, while also expanding its money-movement capabilities to dozens of other countries. Its business model prioritizes low-cost digital acquisition and a broad range of banking services without the overhead of physical branches.

In FY 2025, revenue reached approximately $16.3 billion, a significant growth of 45% over the prior year. The company reported a net income of close to $2.9 billion for the fiscal year. This performance led to a net margin of 18.1%, suggesting that the company is effectively scaling its platform while maintaining a higher portion of revenue as profit compared to many traditional banking peers.
